categories.finding: A hands-on connector demo leads to zip ties, correction controls, mushroom scooping, prototype history and product packages.
The operator and robot workbench are visible immediately, with a hand on a control. The viewer sees a physical demonstration before a brand claim.
Robot teaching/manipulation is visible early and concrete at 26s. The kit versus full-cell offer is only labeled at 241–253s.
Human controls, pedals and robot joints change position; close contact views show grippers approaching and separating. Exact force, speed and easing are not established.
Wide operator views alternate with contact-point close-ups. White chapter cards mark larger topic changes; picture-in-picture supports the scoop explanation.
Exposed cables, bench lighting and unfinished-looking hardware create a practical workshop setting. This is visible treatment, not proof of production readiness.
Most early instruction is not captioned. Late large package labels are clear; the research page is too dense for reading as a whole at sheet size.
The ASR draft supplies detailed method explanation and performance claims; voice pace, emphasis and clarity were not heard.
Music character and structure are unverified.
Effects and their sources are unverified.

categories.finding: The gripper and scoop actions remain visible silently; training logic, benchmark conditions and motor explanation require text or speech.
Close-ups focus on the contact point. Wider demonstrations contain many arms and cables, so labels would help identify controller versus controlled arm.
The long format gives room for repeated attempts and hardware detail. Uncaptioned interview stretches carry little new visual information.
categories.experiment: Add short labels for demonstration, correction and retry states.

categories.finding: The opening promises hands-on robot control; connector and scoop examples deliver visible actions, and the ending names purchasable packages.
Visible attempts and workshop detail appear intended to build trust through process. Actual trust or interest was not measured.
The operator, controller and cell remain traceable through the first task. Chapter cards and new benches clearly mark changes.
Object-handling states are visible. ASR mentions 97% over 100 zip ties and under 40 minutes of data, but the full benchmark and training process are not shown or checked.
The physical controller/arm arrangement, foot pedals and compact frame provide specificity beyond branding.
Contact close-ups and the second task prove visible range. The prototype section adds engineering context but could be separate from a short launch cut.
For Tin, show a human correction, the system’s next output and a repeated task with the correction retained.

lessons.keep: Cut from the whole operator setup to the exact contact point where the task succeeds or fails.
try: For Tin correction learning, show one wrong draft, one human correction and the next matching draft with the corrected detail retained.
For a workflow demo, pair a wide process overview with a close result inset, and label the current stage rather than relying on narration.
lessons.avoid: Presenting a short successful action as proof of a stated benchmark or broad reliability.
lessons.open: Benchmark validity, actual training procedure, force/speed detail, sound and continuous task execution remain unverified.

comparison.story: Robot teaching → precision and flexible-object demos → correction method → second task → prototype → packages.
comparison.motion: Physical controller/gripper/scoop actions shown at 1 fps; exact dynamics and success rates unverified.
comparison.sound: Local ASR draft read for method/claims; no validated listening or sound-layer analysis.
comparison.texture: Practical workshop with exposed hardware, white chapter cards and evidence graphics.
comparison.lesson: A contact-point close-up is stronger explanatory evidence than a wide machine shot.

scope: sampled visual and story review; ASR and measured signal support; no validated audio listening
